series.name: The Night Sky Month by Month

volumes.title: January: The Lantern-Bearer
volumes.text:
I am Mabyn Thrale, and I ring the night hours from the clock tower in Emberwick. This January a boy of nine named Tob came to live with his aunt in the house below. He does not sleep well in a strange town. His aunt asked whether he might sit with me on the leads until the ten o'clock bell, and I agreed, if he wore two scarves. So I am writing down the sky for him, a month at a time.

January is the grandest month to begin. Due south at nine stands the Lantern-Bearer: two bright shoulders, two bright knees, and three stars in a row for his coat buttons. Follow the buttons down to the Lantern itself, the brightest star we have, which flashes blue, white and red because it hangs so low. Tob said it looked like a signal. I said it was: winter, all clear.

volumes.title: February: The Nail and the Ladle
volumes.text:
February on the clock tower at Emberwick, cold enough to squeak. I am Mabyn Thrale, the night bell-keeper, and my pupil is Tob, aged nine, who cannot sleep and has decided to learn the sky instead.

This month I turned him round to face north and showed him the Ladle: seven stars, four for the bowl and three for the bent handle. The two stars at the front of the bowl point straight to a modest star standing alone. That is the Nail. It is not bright, but it is the one star that never moves. Everything else wheels round it once a night, like a cloak swung on a peg.

We tested it. We lined the Ladle up with the weathercock at eight, and by ten it had swung clear, while the Nail sat exactly where we left it. Tob says he likes knowing one thing will stay put.

volumes.title: March: Four Minutes a Night
volumes.text:
I am Mabyn Thrale, who keeps the night bell in Emberwick, and in March my young neighbour Tob came up the tower stairs indignant. The Lantern-Bearer, whom we met in January in the south, had slid over into the west and was setting behind the brewery before bedtime.

Nothing is wrong, I told him. Every star rises four minutes earlier each night. It is too little to notice, but it comes to two hours in a month, and in a year it brings the whole sky round to where it began.

So the winter stars leave by the west door and the spring ones enter by the east. Rising over the Lowlands this month is the Grey Mare, a backward hook of stars for her neck and a blue-white one, the Mare's Eye, at its foot. Tob has begun a notebook. He wrote: four minutes. Check this.

volumes.title: April: The Shepherd's Crook
volumes.text:
April from the clock tower at Emberwick. The evenings are milder, and Tob, the nine-year-old who shares my watch until the ten o'clock bell, has left off his second scarf. I am Mabyn Thrale, bell-keeper, and I am setting down the sky for him month by month.

The Ladle now hangs high overhead, upside down, as if pouring. Follow the curve of its handle onward, and you come to an orange star, warm as a coal. We call it the Hearthstone. It is the foot of the Shepherd's Crook, a tall kite of fainter stars.

Spring skies are sparse. Tob complained that there was less to see than in January, and he is right; at this season we look out through the thin side of the heavens. But the Hearthstone is the first star to show in the dusk, and he spotted it before I did.

volumes.title: May: The Ember Crown
volumes.text:
I am Mabyn Thrale, night bell-keeper of Emberwick, and this is the fifth month of the sky as I am teaching it to Tob, aged nine, on the leads of the clock tower.

May gives us a small thing. High in the east, a hand's breadth from the orange Hearthstone, seven faint stars make a half circle, open at the top like a horseshoe. One of the seven is brighter than the rest, a jewel set off-centre. The town has always called it the Ember Crown.

It is easy to miss, and Tob needed three clear nights to find it without help. On the fourth he found it at once and was cross that he had ever thought it hard. Darkness comes late now. His aunt allows him to stay until the ten o'clock bell only on Fridays, so the Crown is a Friday constellation.

volumes.title: June: The Gate
volumes.text:
June on the Emberwick clock tower, and I, Mabyn Thrale, have very little night to ring the hours through. At midsummer the sky here never turns fully black. A pale glow travels along the northern horizon from sunset to sunrise, and only the stronger stars come out.

That suits this month's lesson, which is three stars and nothing else. Tob, my nine-year-old fellow watcher, found them himself in the east at half past ten, with special leave from his aunt: three bright stars making a tall, narrow triangle, each belonging to a different figure. We call the triangle the Gate. When it stands in the east at dusk, summer has come through it.

The highest and bluest of the three is the Weir-light, which passes almost straight overhead. Tob lay flat on the leads to look at it and fell asleep there, which his aunt counts as progress.

volumes.title: July: The Heron
volumes.text:
I am Mabyn Thrale, bell-keeper, writing the July sky for Tob, the boy who keeps the first half of the night watch with me on the tower at Emberwick. The nights have begun to darken, and inside the triangle we call the Gate a shape has come clear.

It is the Heron. One bright star marks the tail; a long line of fainter ones runs out for the neck, and a shorter line crosses it for the wings. It is flying south with its neck stretched, as herons on the marsh never do, and Tob has complained.

On the darkest nights there is something more. A faint band of light runs the length of the Heron and on to the southern roofs, like breath on a window. That is the Pale River, and the Heron is following it. In September I shall show it to him properly.

volumes.title: August: The Harvest Sparks
volumes.text:
August, and for once I let Tob stay past the ten o'clock bell. I am Mabyn Thrale, who rings the night hours in Emberwick, and on the twelfth his aunt climbed the clock tower with a blanket and a jug of cocoa.

Every year in the second week of August the shooting stars come thick. We call them the Harvest Sparks. They may flash anywhere in the sky, but trace each trail backward and they all seem to spring from one spot in the north-east.

The trick is to lie flat and look at nothing. Tob kept the tally: forty-three in the hour before midnight, one of them bright enough to leave a glowing thread that lasted while he counted four. Each is a speck no bigger than a grain of sand, burning up high in the air. He did not believe me. He wrote it down anyway.

volumes.title: September: The Pale River
volumes.text:
I am Mabyn Thrale, night bell-keeper, and in September I kept a promise made in July to Tob, the nine-year-old who watches with me on the clock tower at Emberwick. We chose a night with no moon. I asked the lamplighter to leave the two lamps in the square until last.

The Pale River ran from the north-east horizon, straight overhead through the Heron, and down into the south-west: a broad, uneven band of soft light, brighter in some reaches than others, split along part of its length by a dark channel that we call the Ford.

Then I handed him my brass spyglass. Wherever he pointed it along the River, the glow broke up into stars, too faint and too many to count. It is all stars, I said. He was silent for some time, which is rare, and then asked very quietly how far it went.

volumes.title: October: The Barn Door
volumes.text:
October on the tower. The dark comes early enough now that Tob, my young fellow watcher, has a full two hours before the ten o'clock bell sends him to bed. I am Mabyn Thrale, and I ring that bell, in Emberwick, every night of the year.

The autumn sky has one plain signpost: four stars in a great square, high in the south, with almost nothing inside it. We call it the Barn Door. It is not bright, but once seen it cannot be lost.

From one corner two curving lines of stars run off north-eastward. Beside them there is a small smudge like a thumbprint on glass. Tob found it by looking slightly to one side, which is the way to see faint things. That smudge, the almanac-maker tells me, is the farthest thing a human eye can see. Tob has underlined it twice.

volumes.title: November: The Goslings Return
volumes.text:
I am Mabyn Thrale, bell-keeper of Emberwick, and November brought my pupil a surprise I had been saving. Tob was nine when he first climbed the clock tower; he turned ten on the third, and came up the stairs that evening in a new coat.

Low in the east hung a tiny knot of stars, like a pinch of frost. These are the Goslings. Most people count six. Tob counted seven straight off, and with the spyglass he gave up at thirty.

They are the first of the winter stars, I told him. Wait an hour or two and the rest follow them up, the same figures we watched leave by the west door last spring. He has been cutting two discs of card, one to turn upon the other, with the Nail at the centre pin. He will not yet say what it is for.

volumes.title: December: The Sky Comes Round
volumes.text:
December, the longest nights. I am Mabyn Thrale, and I have rung the night hours from the Emberwick clock tower through a whole year with Tob beside me. He came last January, a boy of nine who could not sleep in a strange town.

On the shortest day his aunt gave him leave to stay late. At eleven the Lantern-Bearer stood due south: two shoulders, two knees, three buttons, and the Lantern flashing low over the roofs. He stood there at nine last January, and soon will again. Four minutes a night, Tob said, and showed me his card wheel. Turn the top disc to the date and the hour, and a cut-out window shows the sky.

He has pinned it by the bell rope for whoever watches after us. Then he sat down on the stairs to wait for midnight, and was asleep before the bell.

volumes.title: A Drawing in a Copybook
volumes.text:
I am Ottoline Brandreth, schoolmistress at Fellfoot in the Northern Fells. Among my grandmother's things is a child's copybook, and on its last page a drawing in brown ink: the outline of Harrow Fell, and above them a bright head with a long tail swept upward. Beneath it she wrote: The Lantern Comet, drawn by Sabeth Brandreth, aged twelve, from the school wall.

That was sixty-one years ago. Mr Rudd, the almanac-maker in Emberwick, has gone through the old records and reckons that the comet keeps a circuit of about that length. It is due back, he writes, within the twelvemonth, likeliest in spring.

So on the first of October I have begun a vigil. I own a short brass telescope with a wide eye, the kind called a comet-sweeper, and the same school wall. Every clear night I shall search, and write here whatever I find.

volumes.title: How to Sweep
volumes.text:
Fellfoot, October. This is the journal of my watch for the Lantern Comet, which my grandmother saw from this village sixty-one years ago. I am Ottoline Brandreth, the schoolmistress, and I am learning the comet-seeker's trade from a book and from cold experience.

A comet new in the sky is a faint round smudge with no tail. It shows first near the sun's place: in the west after dusk, or in the east before dawn. So I sweep those two quarters. I move the telescope slowly level along the horizon, raise it by half its field of view, and come slowly back, like a ploughman.

It takes an hour each end of the night. I wear two shawls and stand on a hot brick wrapped in flannel. The children have learned that Miss Brandreth yawns on clear mornings, and one of them has started bringing me an apple.

volumes.title: The First False Alarm
volumes.text:
I am Ottoline Brandreth, schoolmistress of Fellfoot, sweeping the sky each clear night for a comet due back after sixty-one years. On the ninth of November, low in the east before dawn, I found a soft round glow in my telescope, and my hands shook so that I lost it twice.

A comet moves. That is the test. From one night to the next it shifts its place among the stars, and a smudge that stays put is something else. I drew the glow with the three small stars beside it, and waited.

Two nights later it had not stirred by a hair. Nor on the third. It is a fixed thing, a faint cloud that has surely sat in that spot since before the fells were named. I have ruled a fresh page, headed it Not Comets, and entered it as number one. I expect the list to grow.

volumes.title: The Bearded Star
volumes.text:
Cloud has closed the December sky above Fellfoot for sixteen nights. I am Ottoline Brandreth, the schoolmistress, keeping watch for the return of the Lantern Comet; and since I could not look up, I looked back.

The vestry chest holds the parish book. Sixty-one years ago the curate wrote: a bearded star seen in the west these three weeks, the tail as long as a hay rake; the people much taken with it, and no harm come. Sixty-one years before that, in a crabbed older hand: a great broom star at lambing time.

So it has come at least twice before, and each time somebody here troubled to write it down. My pupils asked what a comet is. Mr Rudd of Emberwick believes it is a lump of ice and dust that the sun warms into a glowing cloud. I told them that, and that nobody yet knows for certain.

volumes.title: The Gooseberry
volumes.text:
I have found a comet, and it is the wrong one. I am Ottoline Brandreth, schoolmistress at Fellfoot, and since October I have swept the sky for the Lantern Comet my grandmother drew as a girl.

On the twentieth of January, high in the north, a small greenish blur drifted into my telescope. It was not on my list of Not Comets. The next night it had moved a finger's width against the stars, and the night after, another. No tail; only a round fuzz with a brighter pip in the middle, like a gooseberry held to a candle.

I sent its positions to Mr Rudd, the almanac-maker in Emberwick. He replied by the next carrier: a true comet, new to every record he owns, and travelling the wrong way to be ours. He has entered it under my name. In this journal it shall be the Gooseberry.

volumes.title: Pins in the Chart
volumes.text:
February at Fellfoot. The small comet I found last month, which I call the Gooseberry, is fading. I am Ottoline Brandreth; I teach the village school; and my real quarry, the Lantern Comet of sixty-one years ago, has still not shown itself.

Each clear night I mark the Gooseberry's place on my chart with a pin. There are fourteen pins now. They make a smooth curve across the north, each gap a little shorter than the last as the comet draws away from the sun and slows. It never grew a tail. Some do not.

One of my pupils, Wren Hollis, who is ten and has the sharpest eyes in the school, held the lantern for me and asked to look. She found the Gooseberry unaided on the last night anyone could. I could not see it myself. I have put her initials by the fifteenth pin.

volumes.title: The Comet Is Late
volumes.text:
Spring has come to the Northern Fells, and the Lantern Comet has not. I am Ottoline Brandreth, schoolmistress of Fellfoot. I have swept the dusk and the dawn on every clear night since October, and my list of Not Comets has reached nineteen.

I wrote to Mr Rudd in Emberwick to ask whether his arithmetic might be at fault. His answer was kind. Sixty-one years is the comet's habit, he says, not its promise. On its long road out and back it passes the great slow planets, and each one tugs it a little, this way or that. It may be half a year early or half a year late, and no almanac can say which.

Then it rained for three weeks. I mended the telescope case, marked forty slates, and slept, I admit, extremely well. The copybook stays open on my desk at my grandmother's drawing.

volumes.title: Short Nights
volumes.text:
I am Ottoline Brandreth, schoolmistress at Fellfoot, nine months into my watch for the Lantern Comet. It is June, and the sky is against me. Dusk lingers until nearly midnight, dawn begins soon after, and a faint comet would drown in the twilight between.

I came near to stopping. It was Wren Hollis, my pupil of ten, who would not hear of it. She now keeps the log on the nights I sleep, and writes Nothing in a round hand with the hour beside it.

To pass the bright evenings I studied my grandmother's drawing and saw something I had missed. The sun had set to the right of Harrow Fell; the tail streams up and to the left. A comet's tail does not trail behind it like chimney smoke. It points away from the sun, always, whichever way the comet is going. She drew it truly at twelve.

volumes.title: Not the Same as Sparks
volumes.text:
August at Fellfoot, and my whole school lay on the wall to watch the shooting stars that come at harvest. I am Ottoline Brandreth, their teacher, and for ten months I have been waiting for a comet. The children assumed these were what I had been looking for.

They are not, and I used the evening to say why. A shooting star is over in a breath; it is a speck of dust burning in our own air. A comet is vast and very far away. It does not streak. It hangs in the same part of the sky for weeks, creeping a little each night.

So nobody need be afraid of blinking, I said. Wren Hollis asked whether the dust might be crumbs a comet had dropped. I did not know. I have written to ask Mr Rudd in Emberwick, and I rather hope she is right.

volumes.title: A Year on the Wall
volumes.text:
On the first of October I had kept my vigil for a full year. I am Ottoline Brandreth, schoolmistress of Fellfoot, and I began sweeping the sky for the Lantern Comet because my grandmother drew it from this same school wall sixty-one years ago.

The tally for the year: one hundred and forty-one clear nights, twenty-three Not Comets, one small comet nobody asked for, and a pupil, Wren Hollis, who can now find her way about the sky better than I can.

On the nineteenth, before dawn, I was sweeping low in the east over the ridge of Cold Rigg. A dim round glow slid into view beside a pair of stars I know well. There is no smudge there on my list. I drew its place, and the cloud came over before I had finished. I have told nobody. I must see whether it moves.

volumes.title: It Moves
volumes.text:
I am Ottoline Brandreth, schoolmistress at Fellfoot, and for four mornings I taught sums with half my mind out of the east window. A faint glow I had found before dawn was waiting to be proved, and the sky stayed shut.

On the twenty-third of October it cleared at five. The glow had left the pair of stars and stood a thumb's width nearer the sunrise. The following dawn it was brighter, with a short stub of light on the side away from the sun. A tail.

I ran to the Hollis farm in my slippers to fetch Wren, who had earned the sight. Then I wrote to Mr Rudd in Emberwick by the carrier. His answer came in two days: the path fits. It is the Lantern Comet, half a year late, and it will pass round the sun into our evening sky.

volumes.title: The Lantern Comet
volumes.text:
By the first week of December the Lantern Comet had rounded the sun and stood in the west after dark, and all of Fellfoot came out to the school wall. I am Ottoline Brandreth, the schoolmistress. I waited fourteen months for this.

It needed no telescope. The head was a soft bright star beside Harrow Fell, and the tail rose from it up and to the left, longer than my hand held at arm's length. Through the glass there were two tails: one thin, straight and bluish, one broad and curved like a feather.

I drew it on the blank page facing my grandmother's drawing. The two agree in everything but the handwriting. Then I gave the copybook to Wren Hollis, who is ten. She will be seventy-one when it comes again. She has promised to be on the wall, and to bring someone young to hold the lantern.

volumes.title: A Wager at the Heron
volumes.text:
I am Ezra Longbarrow, and I keep the Reedwater Ferry where the river Ember crosses the marsh. I have always known the moon the way one knows a neighbour: by sight, without asking her business.

In January Mr Rudd, the almanac-maker from Emberwick, crossed with me and remarked that no man could foretell the moon without books. I said my eyes were as good as his books. By the time we reached the Heron inn it was a wager. For every full moon of this year I am to write down, beforehand, the day it will fall and the hour it will rise. Ten right, to the day and the half hour, and he prints my table in his almanac and buys the ferry a new bell. Fewer, and I carry him free for life.

Mrs Oake at the Heron holds my sealed slips. The first was a guess. I missed by a day.

volumes.title: Twenty-Nine and a Half
volumes.text:
February on the marsh. I am Ezra Longbarrow, ferryman at Reedwater, and I have wagered the almanac-maker that I can foretell this year's full moons with nothing but my eyes and the ferry-house clock. I lost January's. So I started counting.

I cut a notch in the doorpost each night and drew the moon's shape beside it in chalk. From one full moon to the next came to twenty-nine days and about a half. That gave me the right day for February, and I was proud of it.

But I had the rising wrong by more than an hour. I had supposed the moon kept time like the carrier's cart. She does not. She rises later every night, by three quarters of an hour or so, sometimes less, sometimes a good deal more. Mrs Oake at the Heron opened my slip and shook her head. Two moons gone, none right. I need ten.

volumes.title: She Rises as He Sets
volumes.text:
I am Ezra Longbarrow of the Reedwater Ferry, on the Ember marsh, and I am two full moons down in a wager with Mr Rudd the almanac-maker. In March I found the rule that saved me, and I found it standing in the middle of the river.

It was the evening of the full moon. I was halfway across with a load of withies when I saw the sun touching the reeds in the west, red and flat, and at the same moment the moon lifting out of the reeds in the east, the same size and nearly the same colour. I stood between them like the pin of a balance.

The full moon is full because she stands opposite the sun. So she must rise as he sets. I need only know the hour of sunset, and any ferryman knows that. My slip for March was right in both parts. One.

volumes.title: Ash-Light on the Young Moon
volumes.text:
April at Reedwater. I am Ezra Longbarrow, the ferryman, and I am making a year's table of the moon from my own watching, to win a bet. This month's full moon I called right, which makes two. But it is the young moon I want to set down.

Three evenings after new, she hung in the west as a thin bright curl, and the rest of her disc was there too, faintly, the grey of cold ash. I had seen that all my life and never wondered at it.

My niece Dilly, who is eight, helped me puzzle it out with a lantern and a turnip in the ferry house. The bright curl is sunlight. The grey is light from our own world, shining up at the moon as she shines down on us. It is second-hand sunshine. I have added a column to my table and headed it ash-light.

volumes.title: Two Moons in May
volumes.text:
I am Ezra Longbarrow, ferryman on the Ember marsh, and my wager with Mr Rudd of Emberwick is that I shall foretell ten of this year's full moons. In May I discovered why he smiled when we shook hands.

A full moon came on the second of the month. I counted on twenty-nine days and a half from my doorpost notches and got the thirty-first. I counted again. May has two. Twelve moons take only three hundred and fifty-four days, so the moon's year runs eleven days short of the sun's, and this year a thirteenth full moon squeezes in. Thirteen chances to be wrong, and he never said a word.

I sealed both slips with Mrs Oake at the Heron and got both right. I also marked the tides, which run highest just after full and new; the ferry landing was awash each time. Four right of six. It can still be done.

volumes.title: The Midnight Moon
volumes.text:
June, and a hard lesson at the Reedwater Ferry. I am Ezra Longbarrow, and I have bet the almanac-maker that I can foretell the year's full moons, day and rising, from my own tables. I wrote the thirtieth for this one.

She rose that evening as round as a cheese, low and honey-coloured over the marsh, and I crossed to the Heron inn feeling sure of myself. Mr Rudd was waiting with his almanac open. By his reckoning the moon did not come exactly full until twenty minutes past midnight, which is the first of July.

Mrs Oake, who judges, ruled for the book. A day is a day. That leaves me four right out of seven, with six moons to come, and I can afford no more misses. I have learned that a moon may look full for two nights and be full for only a moment.

volumes.title: The Ferryman in the Moon
volumes.text:
I am Ezra Longbarrow, keeper of the Reedwater Ferry on the Ember, and I must call every remaining full moon of this year correctly to win my wager with Mr Rudd. July's I called to the day and within ten minutes of her rising. Five.

The summer full moon keeps low. She crept along above the southern reeds all the short night, deep yellow, never climbing higher than the top of my ferry pole, and set again before four. In winter she will ride high overhead. She does the opposite of the sun in everything.

With her so low and slow I studied her face. It is always the same face; she never turns her back. The grey patches make a man standing with a long pole, plain as paint. My niece Dilly says it is a heron. We have agreed that it is a ferryman, on weekdays.

volumes.title: Fifty Minutes, More or Less
volumes.text:
August on the marsh. I am Ezra Longbarrow, ferryman at Reedwater, and the table of the moon I am keeping to win a wager now fills the back wall of the ferry house. The August full moon was right, day and hour. Six, with four to get and four to come.

This month I filled in the nights between. Night passengers want to know one thing, whether there will be a moon to cross by, so I timed her rising every evening for a month. On average she is fifty minutes later each night. But the average hides a great deal: I have seen it as little as twenty minutes and as much as an hour and a quarter.

So the table shows, for each night, a small drawn moon and an hour. A drover studied it for some time and said it was the first almanac he had ever been able to read.

volumes.title: The Harvest Moon
volumes.text:
I am Ezra Longbarrow of the Reedwater Ferry, and September's full moon was the seventh I have foretold correctly for my wager with Mr Rudd the almanac-maker. Three more are needed, and exactly three remain.

This is the moon the Lowland farmers love, and now I know why. Around the full this month she rose barely twenty minutes later each evening, for five evenings together. No sooner had the sun gone than the moon was up, big and orange, and the reapers worked on by her light. I ferried four harvest wagons across after supper and never lit the lamp.

It is the season, not kindness. In autumn her path lies low and slanting along the horizon, so a day's travel lifts her little. In spring it is the other way about. I had noticed the long gaps in March and cursed them. Now they have a place in the table.

volumes.title: The Copper Moon
volumes.text:
October at Reedwater, and a night I did not foretell. I am Ezra Longbarrow, ferryman, with eight full moons now called correctly in my wager and two still to win.

Mr Rudd came out from Emberwick himself for this one and would not say why. The moon rose at sunset, to the minute of my slip. Mrs Oake marked it right. Then, towards ten, a dark bite appeared on her left edge. It grew. Within the hour the whole moon had gone the colour of an old copper kettle and hung there dim and round, and the stars came out thick around her.

It is the shadow of our own world, Mr Rudd said, crossing her face. His books had told him the night and the hour years ago. Mine could not have. I took off my hat to the books. He said my table had the rising closer than his.

volumes.title: High and Cold
volumes.text:
I am Ezra Longbarrow, and I keep the ferry at Reedwater on the Ember marsh. For my wager with the almanac-maker I needed November's full moon and December's, both, with no room for a slip. November's is won. Nine.

She rose at sunset, as she must, a little north of east. But what a different creature from July. By midnight she stood as high as the midsummer sun at noon, and the frozen reeds were lit like a field of glass. The winter full moon takes the high road that the summer sun takes, and stays up fifteen hours.

There was a ring around her on the second night, wide and pale. I have learned from the marsh folk that it means snow, and I have learned from this year to write such things down. The table has a remarks column now. Dilly is drawing the moons in it; her circles are better than mine.

volumes.title: Thirteen Moons
volumes.text:
The thirteenth full moon of the year fell on the twenty-fourth of December. I am Ezra Longbarrow, ferryman at Reedwater, and my slip, sealed a month before at the Heron inn, said: the twenty-fourth, rising at ten minutes to four, as the sun goes down.

Half the marsh came to the landing to see. Mr Rudd stood with his watch open. The sun went into the reeds; the moon came out of them; he snapped the watch shut and said eight minutes to. Mrs Oake declared it: ten right of thirteen. The wager was mine.

He has kept his word. My table will be printed in next year's almanac as Longbarrow's Moon for Travellers, and the new ferry bell came by cart on Tuesday. I rang it and took him across without charge. He protested. I told him it was for the eclipse. My eyes are good, but I mean to buy his book.

volumes.title: Five That Will Not Stay
volumes.text:
I am Bryony Wend. Master Corbin Yarrow taught the Emberwick school for forty years, and me among the rest. His eyes are failing now. This October he gave me his notebooks, his brass telescope and an unfinished chart, and asked me to do his looking for him.

His subject is the wanderers. The fixed stars keep their patterns for ever. Five lights do not. They drift among the stars from week to week, each at its own pace, and always along the same narrow band of sky, which he calls the Wanderers' Road. Another way to know them: stars twinkle, and wanderers shine steady.

He has names for all five: the Quick One, the Shepherd's Lamp, the Ember, the Alderman and the Slow Miller. And he has a reckoning, forty years in the making. Next November, he says, all five will stand together in the evening sky. He means to be there.

volumes.title: The Shepherd's Lamp at Dawn
volumes.text:
November, Lantern Hill above Emberwick, an hour before sunrise. I am Bryony Wend, and I am observing the five wandering stars on behalf of my old teacher, Master Yarrow, whose sight has gone dim.

The first on his list needs no finding. The Shepherd's Lamp blazed in the east this morning, far brighter than any star, white and perfectly steady. It threw my shadow faintly on the frost. Shepherds going up to the fells at dawn have set their hours by it time out of mind.

But it never climbs far. Master Yarrow's notes say the Lamp is tied to the sun as a dog is tied to a cart: it may run ahead or lag behind, never more than a few hours either way. So it is a morning star or an evening star and is never seen at midnight. Already it rises later each week.

volumes.title: The Ember Rises
volumes.text:
I am Bryony Wend of Emberwick, keeping watch on the five wandering stars for Master Corbin Yarrow, who taught me my letters and can no longer see the sky. In December I met the one the town is fondest of.

The Ember comes up in the east at about nine these nights, and there is no mistaking it. It is the colour of a coal that has been blown on, a steady orange-red among the blue-white winter stars. It stands at present just beneath the little cluster we call the Goslings.

I marked its place on his chart with the date. A week later it had crept a finger's width to the east, and a week after that, another. That is the proper direction; all the wanderers travel eastward along their Road. Master Yarrow had me read the positions aloud twice. Watch it closely next month, he said, and smiled, and would not say why.

volumes.title: The Ember Stands Still
volumes.text:
January on Lantern Hill, with my feet in a sack of straw. I am Bryony Wend, and I am the eyes of old Master Yarrow of Emberwick in the matter of the wandering stars. Last month he told me to watch the red one, the Ember, and now I know why.

It has been slowing. In December it moved a finger's width eastward each week against the stars. In the first week of January it managed half that. In the second, a hair. And for the last ten nights it has not moved at all; it sits beside the same faint star as though it had forgotten its errand. It is also a good deal brighter.

I reported this to him with some alarm, thinking I had measured badly. He was delighted. Nothing is wrong, he said. It is about to do the thing that puzzled people for a thousand years. Go on marking.

volumes.title: The Ember Runs Backward
volumes.text:
I am Bryony Wend, observing the five wanderers from Lantern Hill for my old schoolmaster, Corbin Yarrow of Emberwick. In February the red wanderer we call the Ember turned round and went the wrong way.

Night by night it slid westward, back past the stars it had passed in December. It rose now at sunset and stood high at midnight, brighter than I had ever seen it.

Master Yarrow explained it at his kitchen table with two walnuts. All the wanderers circle the sun, he believes, and so do we. We are on the inner track and travel faster. When we overtake the Ember, it seems to drift backward, just as a slow cart seems to slide back along the hedge when the mail coach passes it. It is nearest to us then, which is why it burns so bright. He pushed the walnuts round until I could do it myself.

volumes.title: The Loop Closed
volumes.text:
March. I am Bryony Wend, and for five months I have plotted the wandering stars on a chart begun by Master Yarrow, the old schoolmaster of Emberwick, whose eyes can no longer do it.

The Ember has finished its trick. Through February it ran backward; in the middle of March it slowed, stood still a second time, and then set off eastward again as though nothing had happened. I joined my dated marks with a pencil line. They make a flattened loop, like a stitch dropped and picked up. It is fading already as we leave it behind, and he says it will linger in the evening sky until autumn, growing dimmer.

The Shepherd's Lamp, meanwhile, has gone. I looked for it at dawn all month and found only daylight. It is passing behind the sun, he says, and will come out on the other side as an evening star.

volumes.title: The Quick One
volumes.text:
I am Bryony Wend of Emberwick, and in April my old teacher Master Yarrow set me the hardest task on his list of five wandering stars: to catch the Quick One. He saw it himself, he says, only eleven times in forty years.

It keeps even closer to the sun than the Shepherd's Lamp does. It can be seen for a week or two, and only in twilight, in the half hour when the sky is neither light nor dark. Then it dives back into the glare.

I climbed Lantern Hill on six clear evenings and stared at the place where the sun had set until my eyes watered. On the seventh I had it: a small, pinkish, steady spark above the brewery roofs, there for twenty minutes and gone. I ran down the hill to tell him. He made me describe the colour three times. Twelve, he said.

volumes.title: The Alderman and His Clerks
volumes.text:
June over Emberwick. The nights are short, but the fourth of the wandering stars does not need a dark one. I am Bryony Wend, observing for Master Corbin Yarrow, the old schoolmaster, whose eyes have failed him.

The Alderman rises as the sun sets this month and stays up all night: a big, calm, cream-coloured light, brighter than anything but the Shepherd's Lamp. It moves along the Wanderers' Road with great dignity, taking twelve years to go round.

Through the brass telescope it is a small round disc, and beside it, in a straight line, are four tiny stars. Master Yarrow calls them the clerks. I drew them: three on the left and one on the right. The next night, two and two. The night after, only three, the fourth being hidden behind the Alderman himself. They circle him, as he circles the sun. In twelve nights no two drawings matched.

volumes.title: The Slow Miller
volumes.text:
I am Bryony Wend, and since last October I have been the eyes of Master Yarrow of Emberwick, who watched the five wandering stars for forty years. In July I came to the last of them, and his favourite.

The Slow Miller is a quiet, yellowish light, steady, no brighter than a good star. It rises at dusk this month, low in the south-east. It is the slowest of all: it takes twenty-nine years and a half to grind its way once round the Road. In Master Yarrow's forty years it has gone round once and a third.

Then I put the telescope on it. The Miller wears a ring. It is a thin, tilted hoop standing clear of the round body all the way round, like the brim of a hat seen from below. I must have gasped. From his chair on the hill Master Yarrow said: yes. Everybody does.

volumes.title: The Lamp Returns
volumes.text:
September, and dusk on Lantern Hill. I am Bryony Wend of Emberwick. For most of a year I have followed the five wandering stars for my old teacher, Master Yarrow, and tonight the brightest of them came back.

The Shepherd's Lamp vanished into the dawn last winter. This evening, twenty minutes after sunset, it was there in the west, low and brilliant above the marsh. It has passed behind the sun and come out on the evening side, exactly as he said it would.

In the telescope it is not a point. It is a tiny bright shape like the moon a few days short of full. The Lamp shines by borrowed sunlight, as the moon does, and we see more or less of its lit half as it rounds the sun. Master Yarrow nodded when I told him. Four are in the evening sky now, he said. We want only the Quick One.

volumes.title: Closing Ranks
volumes.text:
October again. It is a year since Master Corbin Yarrow gave me his chart of the wandering stars and asked me to be his eyes. I am Bryony Wend, and the Gathering he has been reckoning for forty years is three weeks off.

Each clear dusk I climb Lantern Hill above Emberwick and count. The Shepherd's Lamp stands a little higher in the west each week. Above and to its left is the Ember, small and dim now, a spent coal. Further along the Road is the Slow Miller, and highest in the south the Alderman. Four, strung out like beads. They draw closer together every evening as the sun's glow creeps toward them.

His sums say the Quick One will rise out of the twilight to join them on the eighteenth of November, with a young moon beside. He has had his thick coat aired. I watch the weather as though it owed me money.

volumes.title: The Gathering
volumes.text:
On the eighteenth of November the sky over Emberwick cleared at four, and I walked Master Corbin Yarrow up Lantern Hill on my arm. I am Bryony Wend. For thirteen months I have watched the wandering stars for him, because he taught school for forty years and his eyes are worn out.

As the dusk deepened they came out along the Road, and I named them to him from the horizon upward. The Quick One, a pink spark just over the marsh. The Shepherd's Lamp, blazing. A thin new moon. The Ember. The Slow Miller. And the Alderman, highest of all. Five wanderers in one slanting line, as he had reckoned.

He turned his face to the west for a long time. I can see the Lamp, he said at last, as a sort of smear. And I know where the others are. That will do very well. I marked the date on his chart, and he signed it.
